q: A developer runs `kubectl get pods -n payments` and gets `Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "jane" cannot list resource "pods"...`. Which stage of the API request path rejected the request?
options: Schema validation
Authentication
Admission control
Authorization
explain: The API server knows the user is `jane`, so authentication succeeded (a failure there is a 401 `Unauthorized`). A 403 `Forbidden` naming the user and verb comes from authorization, i.e. RBAC has no rule granting `list` on `pods` in `payments`. Admission only runs for write requests and would show a policy message.

q: You want the same set of permissions (`app-operator`) available in 20 team namespaces, but each team should only get it in its own namespace. What is the idiomatic setup?
options: Twenty copies of a Role `app-operator`, each bound with a ClusterRoleBinding
One ClusterRole `app-operator` and one ClusterRoleBinding per team
One ClusterRole `app-operator` and a RoleBinding in each namespace that references it
One Role in `default` and RoleBindings in every namespace pointing to it
explain: A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole; the permissions then apply only within the RoleBinding's namespace. This defines the role once and scopes grants per namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding would grant the permissions in all namespaces, and a RoleBinding cannot reference a Role from another namespace.

q: Which permissions should you treat as effectively admin-level in a namespace? (select all)
options: `list` on `secrets`
`bind` and `escalate` on roles
`create` on `pods`
`create` on `pods/exec`
`get` on `configmaps`
explain: Creating pods lets you run any ServiceAccount in the namespace and mount any Secret. Listing Secrets returns their values. `bind`/`escalate` let you grant permissions you do not hold. `pods/exec` gives a shell inside running workloads with their credentials. Reading ConfigMaps is low risk as long as you keep secrets out of them.

q: A Deployment applied to a namespace labelled `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted` shows `READY 0/3`, and `kubectl get pods` returns nothing. Where do you find the reason fastest?
options: `kubectl describe replicaset` for the Deployment's ReplicaSet (events)
The kubelet logs on each node
`kubectl get events -n kube-system`
`kubectl logs deploy/<name>`
explain: Pod Security Admission evaluates pods, not Deployments. The Deployment is accepted (with a warning), but the ReplicaSet controller's pod creations are rejected, and the rejection message (`violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest"...`) is recorded as an event on the ReplicaSet. There are no pods, so there are no logs.

q: A pod using an image built with `USER node` and a pod spec with `runAsNonRoot: true` (no `runAsUser`) is stuck in `CreateContainerConfigError`. Why?
options: `runAsNonRoot` requires `privileged: true`
The kubelet cannot verify that a non-numeric user name is non-root, so it refuses to start the container
The `node` user has UID 0 inside the image
Pod Security Admission blocks images with a USER instruction
explain: The kubelet checks the image's configured user against `runAsNonRoot`. A name like `node` cannot be resolved to a UID without reading `/etc/passwd` in the image, so the kubelet fails safe. Use a numeric `USER 1000` in the Dockerfile or set `runAsUser: 1000`.

q: Which statements about ServiceAccount tokens in current Kubernetes are true? (select all)
options: A projected token is bound to the pod and stops working when the pod is deleted
Every ServiceAccount automatically gets a non-expiring token Secret
Pods receive a projected token that the kubelet rotates before it expires
`automountServiceAccountToken: false` can be set on the ServiceAccount or the pod
A token minted with `--audience vault` is accepted by the Kubernetes API server
explain: Since 1.24, tokens are requested via the TokenRequest API, are time-limited, bound to the pod and rotated by the kubelet. Long-lived token Secrets are no longer created automatically. Tokens are audience-scoped: the API server rejects a token issued for `vault`.

q: Your NestJS API only talks to Postgres and Redis. What is the best ServiceAccount setup?
options: A dedicated ServiceAccount with no RoleBindings and `automountServiceAccountToken: false`
A dedicated ServiceAccount bound to `edit` so it can read its own ConfigMaps
No ServiceAccount; set `serviceAccountName: ""`
Use the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount and bind it to `view`
explain: The app never calls the Kubernetes API, so it needs no permissions and no token in its filesystem. A dedicated SA keeps future grants isolated. Every pod runs as some ServiceAccount, so you cannot have none; the env/volume mechanisms deliver ConfigMaps without API access.

q: You applied a default-deny (Ingress and Egress) NetworkPolicy to `shop` and an ingress rule allowing `role=api` → `app=db`. The api pod still cannot connect to `db:5432`, and `nslookup db` fails inside it. What is missing?
options: `hostNetwork: true` on the api pods
A ClusterIP for the db Service
Egress rules from the api pods: DNS to CoreDNS and TCP 5432 to `app=db`
An ingress rule on CoreDNS pods
explain: Default deny covers egress too, so the api pods may not send anything, including DNS queries. Allowing ingress on `db` is only half; the client side needs an egress allow to `kube-dns` on 53/UDP+TCP and to `db` on 5432.

options: Pods labelled `app=gateway` in every namespace
All pods in namespaces labelled `team=web`, OR pods labelled `app=gateway` in the policy's own namespace
Only pods labelled `app=gateway` in namespaces labelled `team=web`
Nothing, because two selectors conflict
explain: Two list items are OR'ed. A bare `podSelector` refers to the policy's own namespace. To get the AND meaning (gateway pods inside team=web namespaces), both selectors must be in the same list item, without the second dash.

q: You created NetworkPolicies on a cluster but connections that should be blocked still succeed. What is the most likely cause?
options: NetworkPolicies only apply to Services of type LoadBalancer
The policy must be in `kube-system`
NetworkPolicies need a restart of kube-proxy
The CNI plugin does not implement NetworkPolicy, so the objects are stored but ignored
explain: The API server accepts NetworkPolicy objects regardless of whether anything enforces them. Enforcement is the CNI's job (Calico, Cilium, kindnet on kind v0.24+, VPC CNI with network policy enabled on EKS). Always test with a real connection.

q: You need to reject Deployments without a memory limit, with minimal operational risk and no extra components. What do you use?
options: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with a CEL expression and a binding
A validating admission webhook written in Node.js
A ResourceQuota
Pod Security Admission at `restricted`
explain: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs inside the API server (GA since 1.30), so there is no webhook to keep available. PSA does not check resource limits. A ResourceQuota on memory forces pods to declare limits/requests, but it is about totals and also affects pods; it is not a targeted rule with a clear message.

q: Which are good reasons to choose Kyverno over plain ValidatingAdmissionPolicy? (select all)
options: You want the policy evaluated without any webhook
You need to verify cosign image signatures at admission
You need to generate a default NetworkPolicy in every new namespace
You only need one simple validation rule
You want background policy reports for existing resources
explain: Generation, image verification and reports are Kyverno features VAP lacks. Running without a webhook and handling a single simple rule are arguments for VAP.

q: shipit-api on EKS must read objects from one S3 bucket. What is the recommended way to give it credentials?
options: Attach an S3 policy to the node group's instance role
Store an IAM user's access keys in a Kubernetes Secret
Map the pod's ServiceAccount to an IAM role via EKS Pod Identity (or IRSA)
Mount `~/.aws/credentials` from the node with hostPath
explain: Pod Identity / IRSA give each ServiceAccount its own short-lived credentials that the AWS SDK picks up automatically. Static keys leak and never rotate; a node role grants the permission to every pod on the node; hostPath breaks isolation and Pod Security.
